title: How Migrating Birds Find Their Way
paragraphs: A blackpoll warbler weighs about twelve grams, less than four sheets of paper.
In autumn it leaves the spruce forest of eastern Canada, flies out over the Atlantic, and comes down three days later in northern South America.
Many of the birds making that crossing hatched a few months earlier.
No parent leads them, and they travel at night over water with nothing to steer by.
Most of them arrive.
The question is not whether such a bird navigates, but what it is reading while it does.
The most informative early experiments did something blunt: they moved the birds.
An animal that merely holds an inherited heading for a set number of days should be unaffected by being carried sideways.
It will fly the same direction for the same time and finish somewhere new.
An animal that knows where the goal sits relative to itself should notice the displacement and turn to compensate.
A large displacement study from the middle of the twentieth century did exactly this with European starlings.
Thousands were caught in the Netherlands during autumn passage, marked, carried several hundred kilometers to Switzerland, and released.
Starlings from that population normally winter in Britain and northern France, reached on a steady heading west and south.
The recoveries split cleanly by age.
Adults that had made the trip before turned and made for the usual wintering range.
The young birds, on their first migration, held the heading they had started with and were recovered in southern France and Spain, shifted by about the distance and direction they had been carried.
That result has held up across species.
A bird on its first migration runs a short set of instructions: fly roughly this way, for roughly this long, then stop.
Heading and duration are inherited, and they suffice, because the route its ancestors flew ends somewhere a bird can survive.
After one full round trip the animal has something better.
It can be carried hundreds of kilometers off course and still correct, which means it has acquired an idea of where it is.
That leaves the narrower question of how a bird points at all.
The oldest answer is the sun.
Using the sun as a compass sounds simple until one remembers that it moves.
Its bearing along the horizon shifts by roughly fifteen degrees an hour, so an animal treating the sun as a fixed marker is off by ninety degrees after six hours.
Birds get around this with an internal clock, correcting the sun's bearing against the time of day.
The clock can be fooled, and fooling it gives one of the cleanest results in the field.
Hold a bird for several days in a room where the lights come on and go off six hours early, and its clock resets to the artificial day.
Release it under the real sun and it departs about ninety degrees from its proper heading, the error running in the direction the shift predicts.
Move the clock the other way and the error reverses.
The bird has simply been handed the wrong time.
Night migrants use the stars.
A caged migrant in the restless state that comes over it in migration season hops and flutters toward the direction it would travel if the cage were open.
Put such a bird in a funnel shaped cage lined with paper that records where its feet land, and the marks pile up on one side, turning a private intention into a measurement.
Under a planetarium sky these birds orient to the projected stars, and rotating the projection rotates the birds.
What a young bird brings to the sky is less than one might expect.
Hand raised birds that never see the sky turn do not develop a usable star compass at all.
Birds raised under a planetarium whose sky rotates around some ordinary star instead of Polaris treat that star's neighborhood as north thereafter.
What is inherited is not a picture of the constellations but a rule for pulling north out of them: watch the sky turn, find the point it turns around, call that the pole.
The pattern itself is learned.
A third cue keeps working when the sky is covered.
Birds in closed cages with no view of sun or stars still orient, and coils that shift the field around the cage turn them predictably.
The avian magnetic compass does not behave like the one in a hiker's pocket.
It ignores polarity and reads inclination, the angle at which the field lines dip into the ground.
Such a bird does not tell north from south.
It tells poleward, where the lines plunge steeply, from equatorward, where they flatten.
Reverse the vertical part of the field and the bird reverses.
Reverse both parts at once, flipping the whole field, and it carries on as before.
How a bird senses the field at all is where the two long running accounts part company.
The first says iron.

Small crystals of magnetite, an iron oxide, have been reported in the upper beak, wired to the brain through a branch of the trigeminal nerve, though the identity of those iron rich cells has been argued over at length.
A field twists such a crystal, and one tethered to a membrane could tug it and open a channel.
The prediction is sharp: a strong magnetic pulse should scramble the crystals and throw the sense off.
Pulsed birds do misorient, experienced ones more than young ones.
The second account says light and chemistry.
In the retina sits a protein called cryptochrome.
When a photon strikes it, an electron jumps to a neighboring molecule, leaving two molecules each carrying one unpaired electron.
Those two electrons stay linked, and the surrounding field tips the pair between two states yielding different amounts of chemical product.
Because the outcome depends on the molecule's angle in the field, and because it sits in the eye, the bird may see direction as faint shading over whatever it looks at.
The compass would then need light, and fail in darkness and under some wavelengths.
In several species it works under blue and green light and fails under deep red.
It also runs on electron spins, which weak oscillating fields in the radio range can upset, fields far too feeble to move an iron crystal.
Birds exposed to them lose their bearings.
It is tempting to treat these two as rivals awaiting a verdict, and the popular telling does.
That framing may be the trouble.
Nothing requires an animal to hold only one magnetic sense.
The eye based mechanism is good at angles and poor at measuring field strength, which makes it a serviceable compass and a useless meter.
The beak and nerve mechanism responds to strength rather than angle, which makes it a poor compass and a plausible instrument for reading position.
A bird carrying both would own a compass and part of a map.
That distinction is the one most often blurred.
A compass answers a single question, which way is north.
It says nothing about where the traveler is standing.
To register a sideways displacement and correct for it, a bird needs a fix: an estimate of its own position relative to the goal.
A map of that kind must be built from something that changes predictably across the ground.
Several candidates exist and not one is settled.
Field strength climbs from the magnetic equator toward the poles, and inclination runs from zero degrees at that equator to ninety at the poles, so two magnetic quantities vary with latitude.
They vary awkwardly.
The gradients are not at right angles everywhere, which makes a two coordinate position hard to extract, and the field drifts over decades.
The gradients are also noisy: iron in the crust can bend the field within a few kilometers, so an animal reading strength alone would sometimes place itself well away from where it stands.
Smell is the other serious candidate: homing pigeons often fail to return from unfamiliar sites when their sense of smell is blocked.
The neatest test of a magnetic map leaves the bird where it is and moves the field instead.
A cage sits inside coils reproducing the strength and inclination of a place the animal has never been.

Some birds shift their heading as though they had been carried there, and in at least one species birds on their first migration do it too, which would mean a rough magnetic map is inherited rather than learned.
Other trials, in other species and other seasons, produce nothing.
It is worth asking why a field this old, and this full of memorable results, has converged so slowly.
Part of the answer is redundancy.
A bird holding sun, star, and magnetic compasses can lose any one and keep flying, so removing a cue often changes nothing and proves nothing.
Part of it is effect size: a twenty degree shift in the mean heading of a dozen caged birds is a small signal, pulled from an animal whose behavior swings with season, fat reserves, age, and weather.
Part of it is that a striking result travels widely and a failed repetition rarely does.
Cue conflict experiments show the trouble plainly.

Shift the magnetic field around a group of birds at sunset, the moment when several laboratories believe the compasses are calibrated against one another, and the birds sometimes adopt the new heading, sometimes ignore it, and sometimes adopt it and abandon it the next night.
Read generously, the pattern says birds weigh their cues rather than obeying any single one.
Read harshly, it says the experiments are not controlled well enough to tell those stories apart.
The more useful question is probably not which cue a bird uses.
It is how an animal carrying several imperfect instruments, each wrong in its own way, combines them into one decision made at dusk with a fixed amount of fuel.
Tracking tags light enough to ride on a warbler are starting to return entire routes rather than a single arrow on a map, and entire routes would settle most of these arguments.
Until then the fair position is that the compasses are largely understood and the map is not.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a bird whose light cycle has been moved six hours before release will
choices: keep its normal heading but leave several hours later than it should
wander without settling on any consistent direction at all
turn and fly in the direction opposite its normal heading
set off about ninety degrees away from its proper heading
orient normally as soon as the real sun becomes visible

proof.quote: lights come on and go off six hours early
departs about ninety degrees from its proper heading

questions.why: Paragraph 6 lays out the arithmetic for you: the sun moves about fifteen degrees an hour, six hours of clock shift adds up to about ninety degrees, and the bird departs that far off, in the direction the shift predicts.
distractorNotes: The shifted clock changes which way the bird points, not when it decides to leave.
The birds still pick a consistent direction after the shift, and only the direction is wrong.
A full reversal would be one hundred eighty degrees, and paragraph 6 gives about ninety.
Seeing the real sun is what creates the error, because the bird reads that sun against the wrong time of day.

questions.stem: In the starling study, the young birds released in Switzerland
choices: kept the original bearing and were found south of the usual wintering range
turned toward Britain the way the older birds did
were carried back to the Netherlands and released a second time
stopped migrating and stayed near the point where they were released
scattered so widely that no shared heading could be read from the recoveries

proof.quote: held the heading they had started with and were recovered in southern France and Spain
normally winter in Britain and northern France

questions.why: Paragraph 3 splits the recoveries by age. The first time migrants held the heading they had started with and turned up in southern France and Spain, shifted by about the distance and direction of the truck ride.
distractorNotes: Heading for the normal wintering area is what the adults did, and the age contrast is the whole point of the paragraph.
No bird in paragraph 3 is returned to the capture site; they were released in Switzerland and left there.
The young birds kept flying, which is why they were recovered hundreds of kilometers away.
The recoveries were consistent enough for the age split to be readable, so they were not scattered.

questions.stem: The passage indicates that the magnetic compass of a bird
choices: works only when the bird can also see the sun or the stars
measures how strong the field is rather than which way it runs
tells true north from magnetic north
reverses when the whole field is flipped at once
reads the dip of the field lines rather than their polarity

proof.quote: It ignores polarity and reads inclination

questions.why: Paragraph 9 says the avian compass ignores polarity and reads inclination, the angle at which the field lines dip into the ground, which is why it sorts poleward from equatorward rather than north from south.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 9 introduces this cue precisely because it keeps working when the sky is covered.
Reading strength is what the beak and nerve mechanism is credited with in paragraph 12, and the passage calls that a poor compass.
True north never comes up; the contrast the passage draws is between polarity and dip angle.
Paragraph 9 says the bird carries on when the whole field is flipped; it is the vertical part alone that turns it around.

questions.stem: The passage reports that weak oscillating fields in the radio range
choices: make the crystals in the beak respond more strongly
throw off the birds although they are too weak to move an iron crystal
restore orientation in birds tested under deep red light
leave caged migrants entirely unaffected
serve as the cue birds use to calibrate their compasses against one another at sunset

proof.quote: fields far too feeble to move an iron crystal
Birds exposed to them lose their bearings.

questions.why: Paragraph 11 uses these fields as the sharp test of the light based account. They disturb electron spins, birds exposed to them lose their bearings, and they are far too feeble to move an iron crystal.
distractorNotes: The passage says the opposite: such fields are too weak to move an iron crystal, so the iron account predicts no effect.
Deep red light is where that compass fails in paragraph 11, and radio fields are not offered as a remedy.
Paragraph 11 says exposed birds lose their bearings in the cage, which is a measurable effect.
Sunset calibration is a separate issue raised in paragraph 17, and nothing there involves radio fields.

questions.stem: Birds hand raised without ever seeing the night sky turn
choices: orient to Polaris without having to learn anything
fall back on the magnetic compass twice as often as other birds
never develop a usable star compass
treat whichever star is brightest as the pole
pick up the star compass later, during the first migration

proof.quote: do not develop a usable star compass at all

questions.why: Paragraph 8 states it plainly: without seeing the sky rotate, the star compass does not develop at all, because what is inherited is the rule for finding the center of rotation rather than the pattern itself.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 8 says the pattern is learned, so no bird arrives already knowing which star marks the pole.
The passage never counts how often birds switch to the magnetic cue.
Brightness is never the criterion; the birds in paragraph 8 learn whichever star the artificial sky turns around.
Paragraph 8 says the compass does not develop at all, not that it shows up late.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 13, "fix" most nearly means
choices: a repair made to a sense that has been damaged
a landmark that stays in one place
a steady heading held without variation
an estimate of one's own position
a workable solution to a difficult problem

proof.quote: an estimate of its own position relative to the goal

questions.why: Paragraph 13 defines the word in the same sentence it uses it: an estimate of the bird's own position relative to the goal, which is the thing a compass alone cannot supply.
distractorNotes: This is an everyday meaning of the word, and nothing in paragraph 13 is broken or being mended.
Paragraph 1 points out there are no landmarks over open ocean, and the paragraph is about a measurement, not an object.
A steady heading is what a compass gives, and paragraph 13 says that is exactly what is not enough.
This general sense fits the sentence loosely, but the paragraph pins the word to position specifically.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 14, "noisy" most nearly means
choices: irregular enough in places to mislead a reading
loud enough to be heard over a distance
unusually strong in the neighborhood of the poles
shifting quickly from one season to the next
carrying more information than an animal could possibly use

proof.quote: iron in the crust can bend the field within a few kilometers
would sometimes place itself well away from where it stands

questions.why: Paragraph 14 explains the word right after using it: iron in the crust bends the field over a few kilometers, so a bird reading strength alone would sometimes place itself well away from where it actually stands.
distractorNotes: This is the everyday meaning, and the paragraph is describing a magnetic field rather than sound.
Strength does climb toward the poles earlier in the paragraph, but that is a separate property from the one this word names.
The drift paragraph 14 mentions runs over decades, not from one season to the next.
The problem described is that the field misleads, not that it offers too much to process.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which conclusion about the inherited program a first time migrant follows?
choices: It is more accurate than what an experienced bird relies on
It is abandoned once the bird reaches the wintering grounds
It supplies a position but leaves the direction to be worked out
It depends on the bird seeing the sun at some point in the flight
It works only while the bird stays on the ancestral route

proof.quote: fly the same direction for the same time and finish somewhere new
because the route its ancestors flew ends somewhere a bird can survive
shifted by about the distance and direction they had been carried

questions.why: Paragraph 4 describes the program as a heading plus a duration, which works because the ancestral route ends somewhere survivable. Paragraph 3 shows what happens when that assumption breaks: carried sideways, the young birds ran the same instructions and landed somewhere else.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 4 says the adult has something better, since it can be displaced and still correct.
The passage credits the adult with an added ability after one round trip, not with dropping the inherited heading.
This reverses the passage: the program gives a direction, and position is the thing it cannot give.
Night migrants in paragraphs 7 and 9 have stars and a magnetic cue as well, so the sun is not required.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from paragraph 12 that a bird equipped only with the eye based mechanism would
choices: be unable to hold any heading after dark
know which way to fly without knowing it had been moved
read its latitude more accurately than its direction
lose all orientation under blue and green light
depend on other birds in the flock to correct its course

proof.quote: a serviceable compass and a useless meter
It says nothing about where the traveler is standing.

questions.why: Paragraph 12 calls the eye based mechanism a serviceable compass and a useless meter of field strength, and paragraph 13 says noticing a displacement takes a position estimate rather than a direction. Put together, that bird could point but could not place itself.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 12 calls that mechanism a serviceable compass, and paragraph 11 has it working under blue and green light.
The paragraph says the reverse: it is poor at measuring field strength, which is what a latitude reading would need.
Paragraph 11 reports that this compass works under blue and green light and fails under deep red.
Nothing in the passage makes navigation a group effort, and paragraph 1 stresses that no parent leads these birds.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Magnetic sensing in birds has now been traced conclusively to a single protein in the retina
Displacement experiments established that migration is entirely learned
The star compass is the single most important cue a night migrant has
Birds use several imperfect cues, and the compasses are better understood than the map
Poor experimental control is the only reason the question remains open

proof.quote: what it is reading while it does
several imperfect instruments, each wrong in its own way
the compasses are largely understood and the map is not

questions.why: The passage moves through sun, stars, and magnetism, then separates a compass from a map in paragraph 13 and closes in paragraph 18 by saying the compasses are largely understood and the map is not.
distractorNotes: The retinal protein is one of two accounts in paragraphs 10 and 11, and paragraph 12 declines to declare a winner, so nothing has been settled conclusively.
Paragraph 4 gives the first migration an inherited heading and duration, so the passage splits inheritance and learning rather than choosing one.
The stars get one stretch of the passage among several, and no cue is ever ranked first.
Paragraph 16 puts redundancy and small effect sizes ahead of method, so control is only part of the story.

choices: argue that the magnetic compass is the most dependable cue of all
explain why the funnel cage produces a readable record of intent
separate knowing a direction from knowing a position
show that a compass is of no use over open water
summarize the evidence for a sense of smell in homing pigeons

proof.quote: That distinction is the one most often blurred.
A compass answers a single question, which way is north.
It says nothing about where the traveler is standing.

questions.why: Paragraph 13 draws the line the rest of the passage depends on: a compass answers which way is north, a map answers where you are, and correcting a displacement needs the second one. That sets up the unsettled map cues in paragraph 14.
distractorNotes: No cue is ranked in paragraph 13, and paragraph 16 explains why ranking them is hard.
The funnel cage belongs to paragraph 7 and has nothing to do with this distinction.
The paragraph says a compass is not sufficient, not that it is useless, and paragraph 1 has birds crossing open ocean successfully.
Pigeons and smell appear in paragraph 14, one paragraph later.

questions.stem: The passage is organized mainly by
choices: opening with a puzzle, splitting it into two problems, then taking each in turn
listing the cues in the order they were discovered and ranking them by importance
comparing birds with other migrating animals at each stage
presenting one decisive experiment and defending it against objections
moving from laboratory work to field work and then back again

proof.quote: not whether such a bird navigates, but what it is reading while it does
That leaves the narrower question of how a bird points at all.
a bird needs a fix: an estimate of its own position relative to the goal
the compasses are largely understood and the map is not

questions.why: Paragraph 1 poses the puzzle, paragraphs 2 through 4 use displacement to split it into holding a course and knowing a position, and the rest of the passage works through the compasses first and the map second.
distractorNotes: The cues do appear in a rough order, but the passage never ranks them, and paragraph 16 says redundancy makes ranking hard.
No other migrating animal appears anywhere in the passage.
Many experiments appear, and the passage weighs them against one another rather than defending any single one.
Cages, coils, and planetariums run throughout, so the passage never divides itself that way.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward treating the two magnetic accounts as rivals is best described as
choices: enthusiastic agreement with that framing
open hostility toward the iron based account
indifference to which account proves correct
confidence that the question has already been settled in one direction
doubt that the contest is the right question to ask

proof.quote: It is tempting to treat these two as rivals awaiting a verdict
That framing may be the trouble.

questions.why: Paragraph 12 calls the rivalry tempting and then pushes back on it, pointing out that nothing requires one magnetic sense and that the two mechanisms suit different jobs.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 12 opens by calling that framing tempting and then argues against it.
The iron based account is handed a serious role in paragraph 12, reading field strength for a map.
The author is not indifferent; the paragraph proposes a specific division of labor between the two.
Paragraph 12 ends with a proposal rather than a verdict, and paragraph 18 says the map is still unsettled.

questions.stem: In accounting for why the field has converged slowly, the author's tone is best described as
choices: scornful of the researchers doing the work
candid about the weaknesses without dismissing the work
unconcerned, on the view that answers will arrive on their own
defensive about criticism coming from outside the field
triumphant that the long argument has finally been won

proof.quote: this full of memorable results
removing a cue often changes nothing and proves nothing
a striking result travels widely and a failed repetition rarely does

questions.why: Paragraph 16 names real problems, including small effects and a published record tilted toward striking results, but it leads with redundancy in the birds themselves. The difficulty is treated as partly built into the subject.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 16 puts redundancy and effect size ahead of any fault in the people doing the work.
The author treats the slowness as a real problem worth explaining rather than something to wait out.
No outside critic appears, and paragraph 17 gives the harsh reading its own fair hearing.
Paragraph 18 closes by saying the map is still not understood.

questions.stem: The passage supports all of the following statements EXCEPT:
choices: A bird that loses one compass can often keep going on another
Magnetic field strength varies with distance from the magnetic equator
Adult starlings corrected course after being carried off their usual route
A bird without its magnetic sense cannot orient at night
Pigeons whose sense of smell is blocked often fail to return from unfamiliar sites

proof.quote: can lose any one and keep flying
Field strength climbs from the magnetic equator toward the poles
turned and made for the usual wintering range
often fail to return from unfamiliar sites when their sense of smell is blocked
Night migrants use the stars.
A bird holding sun, star, and magnetic compasses can lose any one and keep flying

questions.why: Paragraph 16 makes the opposite point: the compasses are redundant, so a bird can lose one and keep flying, which is part of why removing a cue often proves nothing. The other four statements all sit on the page.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 16 says a bird holding sun, star, and magnetic compasses can lose any one and keep flying.
Paragraph 14 says field strength climbs from the magnetic equator toward the poles.
Paragraph 3 says the adults turned and made for the usual wintering range.
Paragraph 14 gives exactly this result as the leading evidence for a sense of smell.

questions.stem: A reader looking for how a bird corrects for the sun's movement across the sky should turn to
choices: paragraph 2
paragraph 3
paragraph 5
paragraph 11
paragraph 16

proof.quote: correcting the sun's bearing against the time of day

questions.why: Paragraph 5 gives the problem and the solution together: the sun's bearing shifts about fifteen degrees an hour, and the bird corrects that bearing against an internal clock.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 2 sets out the logic of moving birds and never mentions the sun.
Paragraph 3 reports the starling displacement and the split between adults and young birds.
Paragraph 11 covers the light based magnetic mechanism in the eye.
Paragraph 16 explains why the field has been slow to settle.
